segments.say: In the nineteen sixties, Britain and France began developing a remarkable aircraft. A passenger jet that could fly faster than the speed of sound, crossing the Atlantic in about half the usual time. It was called Concorde. It was a marvel of engineering, and a symbol of national pride for both countries.

But as development went on, the costs rose far beyond the original estimates. And it became increasingly clear that Concorde would be very difficult to make profitable. Few airlines wanted to buy it. It was expensive to operate, and it was limited in where it could fly, partly because of the noise of its sonic boom.

And yet, the project continued. Part of the reason, many observers have suggested, was the huge amount already invested. Stopping would mean admitting that all that money and effort had been wasted. And so the governments kept going, pouring in more. Concorde did fly passengers, for decades, but it never recovered its development costs.

This story became so well known that biologists and economists sometimes call the sunk cost trap the Concorde fallacy. Continuing to invest in something, not because of its future value, but because of what you've already put in. We met this idea in our last episode. Tonight, let's look at why it traps even very smart decision makers.

One reason is pride. Abandoning a project can feel like admitting you were wrong. And for successful, intelligent people, being wrong in public can feel especially painful. So they may keep going, hoping that things will turn around, and prove them right after all.

Psychologists call this escalation of commitment. The tendency to keep investing more in a failing course of action, especially when we were personally responsible for starting it. In a classic study from the nineteen seventies, the psychologist Barry Staw found that people who felt responsible for an initial decision were more likely to invest additional money into it after receiving bad news, than people who weren't responsible.

In everyday life, this appears in many forms. Holding on to a falling investment, because selling would lock in the loss. Pouring money into repairs on an old car. Staying in an expensive course or subscription, because you've already paid so much. Each time, the past investment pulls us forward, even when the future doesn't look worth it.

One reason organizations sometimes bring in new leaders to review struggling projects is that new people aren't attached to past decisions. They can look at the situation with fresh eyes, and ask simply, given where we are now, is this worth continuing? Without the weight of personal responsibility.

You can try to be your own fresh eyes. Imagine you just arrived, knowing nothing about how much has already been spent. You're offered the choice to start this project, or keep this investment, right now, from this point. Would you say yes? If not, the money already spent shouldn't change the answer.

Another helpful habit is to decide your exit conditions in advance. Before you start a project, or make an investment, decide what would make you stop. If costs rise above this amount, or if this hasn't improved by that date, I'll reconsider. Deciding calmly in advance protects you from the pressure of the moment.

And perhaps most importantly, see stopping as wisdom, not failure. Some of the best decisions people ever make are decisions to stop. To walk away from something that isn't working, and put their time and money into something better. Changing course is not giving up. It's choosing.

So here's what Concorde teaches us. The weight of past investment can keep us going long after we should stop. Feeling responsible makes us more likely to escalate. Looking at the decision with fresh eyes, from today, can help. And setting exit conditions in advance protects us from the pressure of the moment.
